vignette:
He is a 48-year-old Oceania man who comes to therapy with a steady voice and a guarded posture, the kind of man who has learned to keep his face still even when his body is telling a different story. He is married and works as a roofer, a job he has done for years because he is good with his hands, likes honest work, and is used to being high off the ground where he can see everything coming. That sense of control matters to him now more than it ever has.

The assault happens several years ago, after a night out when he is away from home. He does not talk about the details at first, only that he trusts someone he should not have trusted and that, in a matter of minutes, his body becomes something he cannot protect. What stays with him most is the feeling of being trapped and overpowered, of realizing that his strength is not enough to stop what is happening. Afterward, he goes numb. He showers for a long time, then showers again. He does not tell anyone. He tells himself he can handle it, that he has handled worse, that men do not make a fuss about things like this. But the silence becomes its own kind of burden.

In the weeks that follow, he tries to return to work as if nothing has changed. On the roof, the routines help at first: checking the ladder, measuring the line, keeping his footing. Yet he starts to notice how his body reacts in ways he cannot explain. He startles at sudden noises. If someone comes up behind him without warning, his chest tightens and he has to fight the urge to swing around and defend himself. He becomes vigilant in crowded places, always watching exits, always knowing who is near him. At night he sleeps lightly, waking often, sometimes with a jolt and a rush of heat, as if his body is bracing for danger before his mind has caught up.

He begins to avoid anything that pulls him back toward the assault. He stops going out drinking. He finds excuses not to be alone with certain men. He takes longer routes home if he thinks he might run into people from that night. He does not like being touched unexpectedly, even by his wife, and this causes strain between them. He feels ashamed of his distance and more ashamed that he cannot easily explain it. He wants intimacy and also wants to disappear from it. There are moments when he is with his wife and his mind drifts somewhere else, leaving him standing beside himself, watching his own life from a distance.

He has intrusive memories that come without permission. A smell, a tone of voice, the sight of a particular kind of car, even the feel of rough fabric against his skin can bring him back to that night. Sometimes the images are sharp and immediate; sometimes they arrive as a heavy sense of dread with no clear reason. When that happens, he becomes quiet and hard to reach. He says he is fine, but his jaw is clenched and his hands are busy. He works more than he needs to because physical exhaustion is one of the few things that can blunt the images for a while. On the roof, he keeps moving, keeps focusing on the next sheet, the next nail, the next edge, because if he stops, his mind can catch him.

Over time, the changes spread into his mood. He used to be easy to laugh with, but now he finds himself irritable over small things and then guilty for snapping. He feels cut off from people, even people who love him. He does not trust his own reactions, and he worries that the assault has changed him into someone weaker, someone less of a man. That belief is especially painful because so much of his identity has been built around being capable, dependable, and physically strong. He carries a deep sense of betrayal and self-blame, turning the event over and over in his head, searching for the moment when he should have known, should have left sooner, should have done something different.

As he speaks in therapy, it becomes clear that he has spent years surviving by minimizing what happened and by staying busy enough to outrun his memories. Even now, he measures the world for danger without meaning to. He notices where people stand, how close they get, whether a room has only one door. He still gets through the workday, still climbs ladders, still provides for his family, but it takes more effort than anyone sees. Beneath that familiar competence is a man who remains on alert, as if some part of him is still waiting for the moment when he will once again have no way out.
